extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (examining functional claim language)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining claim limitations that use functional language: identify functional language, determine whether §112(f) applies using the three-prong test, construe the limitation under the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI), assess definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), and take appropriate prosecution actions (rejections, suggestions, record-making).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language can appear in limitations that invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and in limitations that do not invoke §112(f). Limitations that do not invoke §112(f) are typically recited with some structure, material or action to define a capability or purpose. Consider whether the phrase describes a feature by its operation/result instead of structural identity. See MPEP 2111 and 2181 and related training modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong §112(f) analysis (invoke §112(f)?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the three-prong analysis in MPEP 2181 to determine whether the claim limitation invokes §112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prong A: does the limitation recite “means” or a generic placeholder for means? (e.g., 'module' may be a generic placeholder). Prong B: is the generic placeholder modified by functional language? Prong C: is the limitation lacking sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function? If Prongs A–C are met, §112(f) applies. Examples: 'color translation module' can be a generic placeholder invoking §112(f) when coupled with functional language; 'aesthetic correction circuitry' may not be a generic placeholder if the specification defines it as a specific circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI when §112(f) is invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: When §112(f) is invoked, the BRI of the 'means-plus-function' limitation is restricted to the corresponding structure in the supporting disclosure, and its equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The corresponding specification disclosure that identifies and links the structure, material or act to the claimed function is considered part of the claim limitation for construction. A reference must disclose the corresponding structure or its equivalent to anticipate the claim. See MPEP and training modules on BRI and §112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI when §112(f) is not invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: When §112(f) is not invoked and an element is recited along with a function, that element is construed as being capable of performing the function; i.e., the BRI of that element is limited by the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between a recited function that limits claim scope and an intended use/result that does not impose structural limits. If the recited structure already performs the function, the functional phrase may simply reflect an intended result and not further limit scope (see examples where boundaries are clear). Record the BRI as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish function versus intended use/result
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between reciting a function compared to reciting an intended use or result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A functional limitation can provide a patentable distinction by imposing limits on the function of a structure/material/action. Typically no patentable distinction is made by an intended use or result unless the use/result imposes some structural or manipulative difference on the recited structure or action. Use this distinction when construing claim scope and when deciding whether the functional phrase limits the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does functional language limit claim scope (anticipation requirement)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the functional language limits the claim scope — i.e., must a prior art reference disclose this functional limitation to anticipate the claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the limitation imposes a functional requirement not satisfied by simply meeting recited structure, then a prior art reference must disclose that function (or an inherent function) to anticipate. If the structure recited in the claim necessarily performs the function, the functional language may not impose an additional limit (and structural prior art may anticipate regardless of explicit disclosure of the function). Examples discussed in the worksheet illustrate both outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness of functional language under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The boundaries imposed by a functional limitation must be clearly defined to be definite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b); language that merely states a result without providing boundaries is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether one of ordinary skill in the art can determine what structure/material/act in the claim performs the function; whether the limitation has well defined boundaries or only expresses a problem/result; and what an anticipatory reference would need to disclose to satisfy the limitation. If boundaries are not reasonably clear, reject under §112(b), identify the specific indefinite language, explain why, and, when possible, suggest resolution. See MPEP 2173.02, 2173.05(g), 2181, 2182.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of corresponding structure for 'means'-type §112(f) limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'means'-type claims, the specification must adequately disclose a corresponding structure/material/act that performs the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate disclosure requires that (a) the corresponding structure/material is disclosed so OOSK will understand what specific structure is identified to perform the recited function; (b) it is sufficient to perform the entire recited function; and (c) it is clearly linked to the function in the written description. If any element is missing, §112(f) limitation may be indefinite or improperly supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner action when functional language is indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines that the boundaries of a claim are not reasonably clear, a rejection under §112(b) should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection must identify the specific indefinite claim language and explain why it renders the claim unclear. The examiner should, when possible, suggest how the indefiniteness may be resolved (e.g., amend to specify structure). Under compact prosecution principles, also consider other applicable rejections (§101, §102, §103, §112(a)). Sample rejection language is provided in the worksheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between §112(b) indefiniteness and §112(a) written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language found indefinite typically lacks an adequate written description under §112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An indefinite, unbounded functional limitation would cover all ways of performing a function and indicate insufficient disclosure to show possession of the invention. Thus, a §112(b) rejection based on functional indefiniteness should often be accompanied by a §112(a) written description rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (102/103) implications of functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language that is not limited to a specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; prior art may anticipate or render obvious depending on disclosure or inherent capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art explicitly discloses the function or a structure that performs the function (same means, equivalent means, or different means that accomplishes the function inherently), anticipation may be appropriate. For §112(f) limitations, the prior art must disclose the corresponding structure or an equivalent to anticipate; non-equivalent structures may render the claim obvious. Examiners must state how they are interpreting the functional term with respect to the applied prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record-keeping and making the BRI clear
rubrics_metrics.description: It is best practice to make the record clear during prosecution by explaining the BRI of claim terms, including any functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When functional language is interpreted (either as means-plus-function or as structural element capable of performing a function), explain the interpretation on the record and how it affects rejections. This includes stating the BRI when applying prior art and documenting assumptions used for compact prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested claim amendments to resolve indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: When functional language is indefinite, applicant can resolve issues by amending the claim to specify how the function is performed, provided support exists in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: specify a particular structure such as 'aesthetic correction circuitry' that performs the function; specify circuitry that modifies signals based on user input; or add disclosed algorithms or structural details from the specification. Amendments should be supported by the specification so that BRI and definiteness are clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural guidance: examine each claim individually and early
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited therein; separate worksheet for each claim; use of worksheet is optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under compact prosecution, each claim should be examined for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review. When functional claim language is found indefinite, make appropriate rejections and consider accompanying rejections (e.g., §112(a)), and address how the functional term is interpreted relative to the applied prior art.
